name: Workers' share of income
question: Are workers receiving a smaller share of economic income as AI develops, and what determines whether productivity gains reach employees, entrants, or owners?
synthesis: Official series document labor-income shares, but their sector coverage, self-employment treatment, and gross-versus-net denominators differ, and they do not identify an AI effect. The reviewed historical literature offers competing accounting, technology, firm-reallocation, and bargaining explanations; early generative-AI earnings evidence remains limited rather than establishing broad wage gains or losses. Innovation can generate worker gains while distributing them unevenly, and negotiated AI protections are institutional responses rather than demonstrated changes in aggregate labor share.

facets.label: Labor share and accounting boundaries
facets.description: Employee compensation, self-employed labor income, sector coverage, depreciation, and GDP/GDI denominators.

facets.label: Productivity-to-pay transmission
facets.description: Whether observed productivity or firm surplus becomes wages, benefits, hours reductions, employment, or owner returns.

facets.label: Who receives the gains
facets.description: Within-labor inequality, incumbents versus entrants, gender, firm sorting, and differences between earnings and ownership income.

facets.label: Rents, concentration, and reallocation
facets.description: Firm-level margins, economic rents, intangible capital, and the movement of output toward firms with different labor shares.

facets.label: Bargaining and contractual protection
facets.description: Worker power, union coverage, negotiated AI rules, and their enforcement and realized income consequences.

facets.label: International and policy context
facets.description: Cross-country measurement, institutional differences, and conditional redistribution or fiscal proposals.

sources.title: Productivity and Costs: Second Quarter 2026, Revised
sources.design: Recurring quarterly national-account and labor-input estimates for major business sectors.
sources.population: US nonfarm business production; not the entire economy or a worker cohort.
sources.duration: Quarterly series from Q1 1947; inspected September 3, 2026 release for Q2 2026.
sources.measure: Labor compensation as a percentage of current-dollar nonfarm business output; compensation includes benefits and proprietor labor estimates.
sources.finding: Q2 2026 labor share was 52.8%, the lowest in this series in the inspected release vintage.
sources.limitations: Sector-specific gross measure subject to revision. Neither a median worker's income share nor evidence that AI caused the decline; not comparable directly with all-economy BEA or ILO percentages.
sources.locator: Release opening paragraphs on real hourly compensation and labor share.
sources.sourceNote: Checked official release, date, level, denominator, and historical claim. No underlying microdata or independent recalculation.
sources.selectionReason: Direct recurring measure of the outcome, with sector and vintage preserved; descriptive national aggregates, not a causal AI study.
sources.headline: US nonfarm business labor share is low, but the series does not identify why
sources.searchOrigin: BLS productivity labor share current release -> Q2 2026 revised.

sources.title: Handbook of Methods: Major Sector Productivity, Calculation
sources.design: Official factor-input and income-accounting methodology, including reconciliation of proprietor returns.
sources.population: Major business-sector accounts and incorporated/unincorporated production.
sources.duration: Current methods page inspected October 22, 2026; no worker follow-up. Publication revision date not established.
sources.measure: Compensation, current-dollar output, labor/capital allocation, and imputed self-employed returns.
sources.finding: Proprietors' mixed income must be allocated between labor and capital using assumptions and reconciliation; recorded employee wages alone cannot represent all labor income.
sources.limitations: Accounting conventions are not causal estimates. Industry labor-cost shares and sector output shares should not be substituted for economy-wide income shares.
sources.locator: Labor compensation; noncorporate capital and labor income; factor-share calculations.
sources.sourceNote: Read targeted methodological sections and imputation equations; year is inspection year, not an asserted publication date.
sources.searchOrigin: BLS labor share definition -> Handbook calculation sections.

sources.title: Estimating the U.S. labor share
sources.design: Official methodological review with historical decompositions of labor share and compensation-productivity growth.
sources.population: US nonfarm business sector and illustrative industry accounts.
sources.duration: Historical illustrations 1947-2015; February 2017 publication.
sources.measure: Compensation/output, proprietor labor imputation, sector exclusions, and price-deflator differences.
sources.finding: The compensation-productivity gap reflects both labor-share change and differing output/consumer deflators; the whole gap is not automatically income diverted to profits.
sources.limitations: Industry illustrations use modified coverage and exclude some proprietor compensation. Historical release values are not current revised estimates or generative-AI effects.
sources.locator: Calculating the labor share; Figure 5; industry contributions; notes 18, 29, 33.
sources.sourceNote: Inspected explanatory sections and tables; methodological review, not an independent new longitudinal AI dataset.
sources.searchOrigin: BLS estimating US labor share Giandrea Sprague.

sources.title: Shares of gross domestic income: Compensation of employees, paid
sources.publisher: BEA National Income and Product Accounts, distributed by Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
sources.design: Annual national-account compensation share; FRED reproduces BEA account A4002E, Table 1.11.
sources.population: Domestic economy's employee compensation, including employer supplements.
sources.duration: Annual recurring series; latest inspected observation 2025, updated September 30, 2026.
sources.measure: Compensation of employees paid divided by gross domestic income; percent, not seasonally adjusted.
sources.finding: The 2025 employee-compensation share of GDI was 50.9% in the inspected vintage.
sources.limitations: Does not add an imputed labor component of unincorporated proprietors' income. Different numerator and coverage from BLS nonfarm business and ILO adjusted shares.
sources.locator: Observations; Notes; BEA Account Code; Table 1.11 link.
sources.sourceNote: Checked official distributor and BEA compensation glossary at https://www.bea.gov/help/glossary/compensation-employees-paid; no raw-table recomputation.
sources.searchOrigin: BEA Table 1.11 compensation share -> official FRED series and BEA glossary.

sources.title: Prototype Measures of Economic Well-Being and Growth: Distribution of Income Between Labor and Capital
sources.design: Archived prototype national-account income split excluding proprietors' mixed income.
sources.population: US domestic income excluding proprietors' income from the denominator.
sources.duration: 1947-2023; last data update April 2024. Discontinuation notice posted March 2025.
sources.measure: Compensation divided by GDI less proprietors' income; complementary gross nonlabor residual.
sources.finding: Under this definition labor's share was 57% in 2023 versus 63% in 1970.
sources.limitations: Not a current live series. Excluding proprietors can conceal changes within mixed income; the gross residual is not solely corporate profits or economic rents.
sources.locator: Section 5, Distribution of Income Between Labor and Capital; discontinuation notice.
sources.sourceNote: Read definition, values, reference years, and archived status; do not compare its level mechanically with 50.9% or 52.8%.
sources.searchOrigin: BEA well-being prototype labor capital shares and definition.

sources.title: SDG Indicator 10.4.1: Labour share of GDP, metadata
sources.design: Official indicator definition, source, imputation, aggregation, and comparability protocol.
sources.population: Employees and self-employed persons across all economic activities.
sources.geography: International country reporting and regional/global aggregates.
sources.duration: Metadata revised March 27, 2026; annual accounting reference periods, not worker follow-up.
sources.measure: Employee compensation plus estimated self-employed labor income, divided by GDP.
sources.finding: The adjusted indicator includes employer social-insurance contributions and imputes self-employed labor income; it is not simply the wage bill divided by GDP.
sources.limitations: Mixed income and missing country observations require modeling. National accounts revisions and source coverage affect comparability; unpaid voluntary work has zero compensation here.
sources.locator: Sections 2, 3, 4.c-4.g and data availability.
sources.sourceNote: Read seven-page metadata definition and estimation sections; did not download country estimates.
sources.searchOrigin: ILO labor income share SDG 10.4.1 -> UN official metadata.

sources.title: World Employment and Social Outlook: May 2025 Update
sources.design: Recurring global labor-market report using national accounts, self-employment adjustments, and modelled recent estimates.
sources.population: Global labor income including employees and estimated self-employed labor returns.
sources.duration: Labor-share comparison 2014-2024; May 2025 vintage includes projections through 2024.
sources.measure: Adjusted labor income as a percentage of GDP, not employee pay alone.
sources.finding: Estimated global labor share fell from 53.0% in 2014 to 52.4% in 2024, a 0.6-percentage-point change.
sources.limitations: Recent endpoint is projected/modelled and revisable. This historical aggregate does not attribute the decline to generative AI or establish identical country trends.
sources.locator: Labour income share discussion; Figure 6 and footnote 13, printed p. 7.
sources.sourceNote: Checked report text, figure context, dates, and projection caveat; no claim this is the latest available ILO vintage.
sources.selectionReason: Direct global measure provides geographic breadth and an explicit self-employment adjustment, with modelling limits visible.
sources.headline: ILO estimates a modest global share decline, not an identified AI effect
sources.searchOrigin: ILO global labor income share 2025 -> WESO May update PDF.

sources.title: Perspectives on the Labor Share
sources.design: Review of labor-share measurement and competing macroeconomic explanations.
sources.population: US and international aggregate/industry evidence discussed in the article.
sources.duration: Historical evidence through 2022 summarized in the publisher abstract; no new worker follow-up.
sources.measure: Labor income/output and explanations involving technology, markets, and globalization.
sources.finding: The review treats labor-share decline as an important empirical pattern but emphasizes that explaining its causes requires resolving measurement and mechanism questions.
sources.limitations: Review is not a new causal estimate of AI; full text was not available through the inspected publisher route.
sources.locator: Publisher abstract and article metadata.
sources.sourceNote: Abstract-only assessment; not a full synthesis of every cited paper.
sources.searchOrigin: Karabarbounis Perspectives Labor Share JEP 2024.

sources.title: Revisiting the Global Decline of the (Non-Housing) Labor Share
sources.design: Cross-country accounting harmonization addressing sector boundaries, housing, and self-employment.
sources.population: Major advanced economies' non-housing income accounts.
sources.geography: Advanced economies, including United States and Canada.
sources.duration: Historical country series; exact country-specific windows not established from inspected abstract. Published 2020.
sources.measure: Comparable non-housing labor shares after accounting adjustments.
sources.finding: The authors find stable or rising comparable shares in major advanced economies except the United States and Canada.
sources.limitations: This does not refute every differently defined global series. Abstract-only access limits appraisal of sensitivity checks and individual country windows.
sources.locator: Publisher abstract.
sources.sourceNote: Primary publisher abstract inspected; not presented as full-paper review.
sources.selectionReason: A substantive counterpoint to universal-decline claims; selection is for accounting relevance, with abstract-only access explicitly disclosed.
sources.headline: Cross-country decline depends on harmonized accounting boundaries
sources.searchOrigin: Gutierrez Piton revisiting global nonhousing labor share primary publisher.

sources.title: Has the Labour Share Declined? It Depends
sources.authors: Taehyoung Cho, Soobin Hwang, Paul Schreyer
sources.design: Accounting comparison of gross production versus net-income labor shares, including asset-price effects.
sources.population: National income accounts in the countries examined, with particular attention to Korea.
sources.duration: Roughly two preceding decades as described in abstract; exact country windows not extracted. January 28, 2017 release.
sources.measure: Labor share under gross/net denominators and alternative capital-income treatments.
sources.finding: The abstract reports a small decline in gross production shares and little or no decline in net-income shares; land and asset valuations matter.
sources.limitations: Definition-dependent historical finding, not a universal absence of wage pressure or evidence on generative AI.
sources.locator: OECD abstract and publication metadata.
sources.sourceNote: Publisher abstract inspected; full working-paper calculations not audited.
sources.searchOrigin: OECD Has the Labour Share Declined It Depends.

sources.title: The Fall of the Labor Share and the Rise of Superstar Firms
sources.authors: David Autor, David Dorn, Lawrence F. Katz, Christina Patterson, John Van Reenen
sources.publisher: Quarterly Journal of Economics, author-hosted published PDF
sources.design: Firm-panel decompositions and industry concentration comparisons with a heterogeneous-firm model.
sources.population: Economic Census firms in six sectors; supplementary international evidence.
sources.duration: 1982-2012 for four sectors; 1992-2012 for finance and utilities/transportation.
sources.measure: Payroll/compensation shares, value added or sales, concentration, and between/within-firm reallocation.
sources.finding: Reallocation toward larger, productive firms with low labor shares contributes substantially to aggregate share declines; the typical firm's change need not match the aggregate.
sources.limitations: Concentration correlations do not by themselves establish anticompetitive conduct. Historical evidence predates generative AI; sector measures are not interchangeable.
sources.locator: Introduction; data; Tables IV-V and Figures VII-VIII.
sources.sourceNote: Targeted reading of theory, coverage, and decompositions, not a replication.
sources.searchOrigin: Autor superstar firms labor share author published PDF.

sources.title: The Elusive Explanation for the Declining Labor Share
sources.design: Review and assessment of competing explanations for historical factor-share changes.
sources.population: Macro and industry evidence synthesized across published studies.
sources.duration: Historical literature available by 2022; no independent follow-up.
sources.measure: Explanations involving technology, trade, market power, bargaining, and demographic change.
sources.finding: Many plausible mechanisms have support, but accounting for their combined contributions remains difficult and can overexplain the aggregate decline.
sources.limitations: Not a causal estimate of any one mechanism or of generative AI; the inspected page exposed the abstract, not the full article body.
sources.locator: Publisher abstract.
sources.sourceNote: Access level deliberately limited to abstract; cited papers not all independently checked.
sources.searchOrigin: Grossman Oberfield elusive explanation declining labor share.

sources.title: Labor Share Decline and Intellectual Property Products Capital
sources.authors: Dongya Koh, Raul Santaeulalia-Llopis, Yu Zheng
sources.design: Historical national-account decomposition emphasizing capitalization of intellectual-property products.
sources.population: US national income and capital accounts.
sources.duration: Approximately ninety years of historical accounts; November 2020 publication. Exact endpoints not extracted from abstract.
sources.measure: Labor share under alternative treatment of intellectual-property investment.
sources.finding: The authors attribute the measured historical decline to the accounting treatment of intellectual-property products in their reconstruction.
sources.limitations: An accounting interpretation under particular conventions, not settled proof that workers experienced no losses. No generative-AI adoption treatment or direct distributional welfare estimate.
sources.locator: Publisher abstract and article metadata.
sources.sourceNote: Abstract inspected; underlying national-account reconstruction not reproduced.
sources.searchOrigin: Koh Santaeulalia-Llopis Zheng labor share intellectual property primary.

sources.title: The Declining Worker Power Hypothesis: An Explanation for the Recent Evolution of the American Economy
sources.publisher: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Spring 2020
sources.design: Macro model and descriptive micro/industry evidence on worker rent capture and wage premia.
sources.population: US employees, industries, and geographic aggregates; multiple datasets.
sources.duration: Long-run changes since the early 1980s through pre-2020 observations; dataset endpoints vary.
sources.measure: Union and large-firm wage premia, worker rents, labor share, profitability, and unemployment.
sources.finding: The authors argue that declining worker power can jointly explain weaker labor shares, higher profitability, and other macro patterns, offering an alternative to product-market monopoly explanations.
sources.limitations: Multiple changing mechanisms and observational evidence prevent a clean single causal decomposition. Not a generative-AI effect estimate.
sources.locator: Abstract; introduction; worker-rent evidence and interpretation.
sources.sourceNote: Targeted paper inspection, not all appendices or discussants' claims. Model interpretation kept distinct from observed correlations.
sources.searchOrigin: Stansbury Summers declining worker power Brookings published paper.

sources.title: Broadening the Gains from Generative AI: The Role of Fiscal Policies
sources.authors: Fernanda Brollo, Era Dabla-Norris, Ruud de Mooij, Daniel Garcia-Macia, Tibor Hanappi, Li Liu, Anh D. M. Nguyen
sources.publisher: International Monetary Fund, Staff Discussion Note 2024/002
sources.design: Policy analysis of fiscal and social-protection responses under uncertain AI labor/capital effects.
sources.population: Conceptual national tax and transfer systems; no treated worker sample.
sources.duration: June 17, 2024 publication; prospective policy options, no outcome follow-up.
sources.measure: Potential distributional effects and policy instruments, not observed labor-share treatment effects.
sources.finding: The note proposes adapting protection and tax systems to spread AI gains while preserving beneficial innovation.
sources.limitations: Conditional policy reasoning is neither a forecast with demonstrated accuracy nor an evaluation of implemented redistribution.
sources.locator: Official publication summary and metadata.
sources.sourceNote: Official summary inspected; no full-paper fiscal calibration or legal-country recommendations independently reviewed.

sources.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
sources.design: Task-based macroeconomic model calibrated to exposure and experimental task-cost evidence.
sources.population: Modeled US tasks, production, and labor/capital income; not an observed national adoption experiment.
sources.duration: October 2024 accepted manuscript; conditional ten-year projection horizon.
sources.measure: Projected productivity and labor/capital income distribution under specified assumptions.
sources.finding: Task savings need not produce very large aggregate gains, and AI can widen the capital-labor income gap even when some less-skilled workers become more productive.
sources.limitations: Forecast depends on automatable-task coverage, costs, new tasks, and adoption assumptions. It does not establish that the projected distributional changes have occurred.
sources.locator: Summary; task framework and macro implications.
sources.sourceNote: Targeted accepted-version inspection; earlier working-paper numeric forecasts were not mixed into this version.
sources.searchOrigin: Acemoglu Simple Macroeconomics AI accepted manuscript author.

sources.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI
sources.design: Survey/register worker panel; difference-in-differences.
sources.population: Eleven exposed occupations.
sources.duration: 2021-2024; March 2026 revision.
sources.measure: Earnings and hours, not national labor share.
sources.finding: Limited average earnings effects despite task change.
sources.limitations: Nonrandom adoption; short horizon; no employer-surplus denominator.
sources.locator: Abstract; administrative outcomes.
sources.sourceNote: Same study as work-humlum-2026; not independent evidence.
sources.selectionReason: Direct realized-pay counterpoint to productivity-based predictions.
sources.headline: Task change need not immediately translate into higher pay
sources.searchOrigin: RFBerlin revised paper; see work extraction.

sources.title: Union Members: 2025
sources.design: Annual CPS household-survey estimates of union membership, representation, and earnings.
sources.population: Employed wage and salary workers; earnings comparisons use the release's specified full-time groups.
sources.duration: Comparable series starts 1983; 2025 estimates use eleven months excluding October. Release February 18, 2026.
sources.measure: Union membership and representation rates, distinct from causal bargaining power or labor share.
sources.finding: 2025 union membership was 10.0% of wage and salary workers; representation is a broader measure and must not be conflated with membership.
sources.limitations: October noncollection due to shutdown makes 2025 not strictly comparable with normal annual averages. Union/nonunion earnings gaps reflect composition as well as possible bargaining effects.
sources.locator: Opening paragraphs; shutdown-impact box; earnings discussion.
sources.sourceNote: Official release inspected; no union wage premium treated as randomized or AI-specific.

sources.title: Rent-Sharing, Holdup, and Wages: Evidence from Matched Panel Data
sources.authors: David Card, Francesco Devicienti, Agata Maida
sources.design: Matched worker-firm panel with worker-match effects and instruments based on outside-region industry revenues.
sources.population: Selected private-sector workers and firms; excludes apprentices, managers, part-time workers, and very small firms.
sources.duration: 1995-2001; October 2011 working paper, preceding 2014 journal publication.
sources.measure: Worker wages, firm quasi-rents, and treatment of required capital costs.
sources.finding: Wages respond to firm rents, but the results do not support workers appropriating the normal return needed to finance capital.
sources.limitations: Instrument exclusion and sample selection are substantive assumptions. Historical rent sharing is not evidence about generative AI or entrants excluded from the sample.
sources.locator: Abstract; Section III, Data; rent-sharing estimates.
sources.sourceNote: Inspected author-hosted working-paper data/design/results; later journal version not independently assessed.
sources.searchOrigin: Card Devicienti Maida rent sharing matched panel author PDF.

sources.title: Who Profits from Patents? Rent-Sharing at Innovative Firms
sources.authors: Patrick Kline, Neviana Petkova, Heidi Williams, Owen Zidar
sources.publisher: Quarterly Journal of Economics, author-hosted published PDF
sources.design: Linked firm/worker tax panel comparing initial patent allowances and rejections; allowance instruments firm surplus.
sources.population: Patent-applicant firms and their workers, including incumbents and entrants.
sources.duration: Applications roughly 2001-2011; business tax records 1997-2014. Published 2019; corrigendum March 10, 2021.
sources.measure: Firm surplus, employment, earnings, retention, and distribution of gains.
sources.finding: Valuable patent allowances raise firm outcomes and worker compensation; gains favor incumbents, men, and higher earners, while entry wages show little response.
sources.limitations: Conditional idiosyncratic-allowance assumptions, not randomized AI. Corrigendum changes structural calibration; reduced-form findings are not an economy-wide labor-share estimate.
sources.locator: Abstract; Sections III-IV; Table VII; 2021 corrigendum.
sources.sourceNote: Read key methods/results and https://eml.berkeley.edu/~pkline/papers/KPWZ_Corrigendum.pdf; omitted superseded structural figures.
sources.selectionReason: Quasi-experimental historical mechanism evidence shows that innovation rents can reach workers unevenly, without labeling patent evidence generative AI.
sources.headline: Innovation gains can reach incumbents without raising entrants' wages
sources.searchOrigin: Patrick Kline author publication list -> published PDF and corrigendum.

gaps.title: A common accounting bridge is needed before comparing headline shares
gaps.summary: Different official percentages cannot be read as competing measurements of an identical workers' share.
gaps.basis: BLS nonfarm business, BEA employee/GDI, BEA's archived proprietor-excluding prototype, and ILO's self-employment-adjusted GDP share have different boundaries. OECD and cross-country studies show that net/gross and housing choices can change trends, not just levels.
gaps.next: Publish a versioned bridge table showing numerator, denominator, sector, benefits, self-employed imputation, housing, depreciation, observation period, revisions, and uncertainty; report harmonized and native series side by side.

gaps.title: Identify AI's contribution rather than attributing long-run declines to it
gaps.summary: The reviewed official series and historical mechanisms do not isolate generative AI's effect on aggregate labor share.
gaps.basis: Historical firm reallocation, worker-power changes, and accounting explanations predate ChatGPT. The macro AI paper is conditional modeling; the Danish panel measures pay without a firm-value-added denominator.
gaps.next: Link verified adoption and usage to firm value added, payroll including benefits, contractor payments, capital costs, profits, output prices, and worker mobility; use phased rollout or credible instruments and aggregate entry/exit effects.

gaps.title: Measure which workers capture gains, not only the labor total
gaps.summary: An unchanged aggregate labor share can coexist with unequal earnings gains, and wage changes alone do not measure ownership returns or household welfare.
gaps.basis: Patent evidence favors particular incumbents; Italian rent-sharing evidence excludes several entrant groups; Danish averages are limited. These findings concern different populations and cannot establish a universal pass-through rate.
gaps.next: Estimate worker-level pass-through by tenure, gender, occupation, contract status, and starting wage, together with benefits, equity income, hours, entry wages, and employer switching; report both within-labor and labor-versus-capital distribution.

gaps.title: Evaluate bargaining protections and policy implementation
gaps.summary: Negotiated AI rules and fiscal proposals establish possible channels for sharing gains, not demonstrated income effects.
gaps.basis: WGA and SAG-AFTRA documents describe rights and contract terms; union membership measures coverage imperfectly; worker-power research supports a mechanism but does not evaluate these AI agreements. IMF recommendations are prospective.
gaps.next: Track covered and comparable uncovered workers before and after implementation, including licences, consent, credits, claims, enforcement, actual payments, hiring, and work volume; extend beyond US entertainment and measure nonunion settings.

reviewNotes: AI-assisted bounded scoping scan, not a systematic review, comprehensive literature census, replication, or human-reviewed evidence label.
Source counts include series, methodological definitions, studies, reviews, institutional frameworks, and a policy proposal. They are not counts of independent causal estimates.

Primary-fulltext denotes targeted sections inspected, not every appendix. Several important accounting counterparts are primary-abstract; their effect sizes and robustness require further fulltext review.
National income time series are repeated measurements, not longitudinal worker panels. Same-worker/firm studies are longitudinal; reviews, definitions, forecasts, and contracts have temporal none.
All numeric claims preserve an observation period and denominator. Release dates, source-version years, model projection horizons, and check dates must not be merged.

BLS 52.8%, BEA 50.9%, and BEA prototype 57% describe different concepts and years. ILO includes estimated self-employed labor income. Gross nonlabor residual is not synonymous with corporate profits or pure economic rents.

Labor-share declines can coexist with rising absolute compensation; average wages can rise through composition while entrants lose opportunities. Aggregate labor share says little by itself about median workers, unpaid work, transfers, or household ownership income.
The latest inspected BLS and BEA pages are revision-prone live URLs. ILO May 2025 is an explicitly dated selected vintage, not a claim of latest global data.
The patent study's 2021 corrigendum affects structural calibration; this scan uses qualitative reduced-form distributional findings and does not repeat superseded structural values.
Generative-AI attribution is especially limited: historical IP capitalization, patents, worker power, or industry reallocation are mechanisms and context, not observed ChatGPT effects.
Humlum-Vestergaard appears in both topic collections but is one study family. WGA 2023/2026 rules and BLS release/method records likewise must not be counted as independent replications.

Geographic coverage is strongest for US/advanced-economy formal work, with Italian microdata and global ILO accounting. Informal earnings, lower-income-country bargaining, and ownership distribution need additional direct evidence.
Contract and policy records describe institutional content, not demonstrated implementation or income effects.
